title: Scattered strips and the rationality of the open field
bodyMd:
In the open-field villages of medieval northern Europe a peasant's arable holding was not a compact block. It lay in a dozen or two dozen narrow strips distributed across two or three great fields, so that a man with fifteen acres might walk a mile between the first of them and the last. The arrangement is costly in every obvious way. Ploughs and carts are dragged further; a headland is wasted at the end of every strip; and a holding so dispersed cannot be watched by one pair of eyes. For a long time historians took the pattern as evidence that medieval agriculture was governed by inherited custom rather than by calculation.

The most influential rebuttal argues that scattering was insurance. Hazards in an open field are local: hail flattens one furlong and spares the next, low ground floods, light soils burn in a dry June. A holding spread across many parcels harvests the average of the village's fortunes rather than the fortune of a single spot. A household living close to subsistence, for which one failed year is not a lean year but a catastrophe, should rationally accept a lower expected yield in exchange for a narrower spread of outcomes. On this reading the peasant was not an unreflective traditionalist but a careful buyer of an expensive policy.

The account has not gone unchallenged. Cheaper insurance was available — granaries, obligations owed among kin, sowing several grains in the same field — and it is not obvious why a costly method would be preferred to them. Reconstructions of actual medieval yields suggest that the variance scattering removed was modest beside the transport and supervision it cost. And scattering was as thorough in districts of uniform soil and gentle weather, where the hazards it supposedly answered were slightest, as in districts where those hazards were severe.

What is unsatisfying about the dispute is its shape. Both sides hunt for the motive behind a practice that persisted for six centuries across terrain of enormous variety, as though a single motive were the sort of thing such a practice could have. The more tractable question is what held scattering in place once it existed: inheritance customs that divided parcels among heirs at every generation, and common rights of grazing over the stubble that obliged each holder to crop in step with his neighbours. A practice may be maintained by forces quite unlike those that produced it, and the second question can be answered from the records even where the first cannot.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage in economic history. It describes the medieval open-field pattern in which one household's arable land lay in many scattered narrow strips; the traditional reading of that pattern as custom rather than calculation; the influential counter-argument that scattering was a deliberate purchase of insurance against localized hazards; three objections to that counter-argument concerning cheaper alternatives, the modest variance actually removed, and the presence of scattering in low-hazard districts; and the author's view that the dispute is wrongly shaped and that the better question concerns what maintained the practice rather than what caused it. No figures, tables or mathematical notation appear.

provenance.notes: Written from scratch for this item bank. Not adapted from, and not a paraphrase of, any LSAC passage or any published article. The open-field scattering puzzle and the risk-reduction response to it are long-standing general topics in agrarian economic history; no historian is named, no position is attributed to a particular scholar, and the wording, structure and the closing argument about maintenance versus origin are the author's own.
